questions.q: What is the narrator's profession and how long had he prepared for this voyage?
questions.a: The narrator is a 37-year-old businessman who, along with his wife, spent 16 years honing seafaring skills in British waters before the voyage. A wrong answer (e.g., "he was a professional sailor" or "he had no experience") reveals confusion between his amateur status and his serious preparation, missing the text's emphasis on deliberate skill-building over decades.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the narrator says "I accepted my approaching death, and as I was losing consciousness, I felt quite peaceful" after being thrown overboard.
questions.a: The narrator experiences a moment of calm resignation when he believes death is inevitable, which contrasts with his later frantic efforts to survive. This shows his mental clarity and lack of panic even in extremis. A wrong answer that calls this "giving up" misses the nuance: he feels peace *because* he has done everything possible, and this momentary acceptance actually conserves energy for his unexpected return to the ship.

questions.q: Using the text, identify three specific actions the narrator takes to keep Wavewalker afloat after the wave strike, and explain the nautical reasoning behind each.
questions.a: 1. Stretches canvas and secures waterproof hatch covers over gaping holes (deflects water overboard). 2. Connects the spare electric pump under the chartroom floor (bypasses blocked hand pumps and short-circuited main pump). 3. Heaves-to with improvised sea anchor (nylon rope and paraffin barrels) to present undamaged port hull to waves, reducing stress on shattered starboard side. A wrong answer that lists generic "pumping" or "steering" without technical specificity shows inability to extract precise, evidence-based details.

questions.q: Compare the narrator's internal monologue during the crisis with his external communication to the crew and family. What does this gap reveal about his leadership style?
questions.a: Internally, he feels "the end was very near" and lacks conviction in his own navigation calculations ("a conviction I did not feel"). Externally, he gives clear orders ("Take the wheel", "steer 185 degrees") and reassures his son. This gap reveals a leader who compartmentalizes fear to maintain morale and operational focus — a hallmark of effective crisis leadership. A wrong answer that claims he "wasn't afraid" ignores textual evidence of his private terror.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The narrator's greatest strength is his technical knowledge of sailing." Use evidence from the text to support or refute.
questions.a: Refuted. While his seamanship is essential (he calculates position with a faulty compass, improvises a sea anchor), the text foregrounds his emotional resilience and familial love as equally vital. He is motivated by "a seven-year-old girl who did not want us to worry" and a "six-year-old boy who was not afraid to die." His technical skill is the tool; his humanity is the engine. A wrong answer that agrees overlooks the story's thematic core: survival is a collective, emotional act, not just a technical one.

questions.q: Write a 100-word diary entry from the narrator's perspective on the night of January 5, capturing his physical exhaustion, mental state, and the moment Jonathan and Suzanne hug him.
questions.a: A strong entry will use first-person voice, reference specific physical details (cracked ribs, blood, cold), show the shift from despair ("end was very near") to the children's unexpected affirmation ("best daddy... best captain"), and end with renewed determination. A weak entry will summarize events without interiority, miss the emotional pivot, or use modern language inconsistent with the 1976 setting.
